title: Split Array Largest Sum
corePattern: Binary Search on Answer (Parametric Search) + Greedy Feasibility Check
interviewTips: Clarify constraints: can subarrays be empty? No, k non-empty contiguous partitions; ask if nums can contain negatives/zeros (here nums[i] >= 0, critical for greedy).
Trade-off: DP O(n^2*k) is intuitive and works for n=1000 but binary search O(n log sum) is optimal; explain why greedy check is valid only for non-negative numbers.
Edge-case tip: answer fits in 32-bit but intermediate sum needs 64-bit (n*1e6 up to 1e9); test k==1, k==n, all zeros, and max(nums) vs sum(nums) bounds.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Dynamic Programming with Prefix Sum
approaches.intuition: Try every possible last cut. If first p elements are split into j-1 parts optimally, and elements p..i-1 form the last part, the cost is max of those two. Take minimum over all p.
approaches.theory: Let prefix[i] be sum of first i elements. Define dp[i][j] = minimal largest sum to split first i elements into j parts. Recurrence: dp[0][0]=0, dp[i][j]=min_{p in [j-1,i-1]} max(dp[p][j-1], prefix[i]-prefix[p]). This enumerates all partitions, so optimal substructure holds. Answer is dp[n][k].

timeComplexity.explanation: n states for prefix length times k partitions times O(n) scan over previous cut p. For n=1000, k=50 this is up to 50M operations.

spaceComplexity.explanation: dp table (n+1)*(k+1) plus O(n) prefix sum. Can be optimized to O(n) with rolling j dimension but need full p loop.

steps: dp[5][2]=min_p max(dp[p][1], 32-prefix[p]): p=3 gives max(14,18)=18 minimal
answer dp[5][2]=18 corresponding to cut after index 2: [7,2,5]|[10,8]

edgeCases: k==1: answer is sum(nums), dp reduces to single row
k==n: answer is max(nums), each element its own subarray
zeros in nums: prefix duplicates, max logic still correct
large sum up to 1e9: use long long, cast to int only at return

approaches.name: Approach 2: Optimal Binary Search on Answer + Greedy Check
approaches.intuition: Guess the answer M = largest allowed subarray sum. Greedily pack as many elements as possible per subarray without exceeding M; this uses minimal number of subarrays. If we need <=k subarrays, M is feasible.
approaches.theory: Feasibility predicate F(M) = can split into <=k parts with each sum <=M is monotone: if M feasible, any M'>M feasible. Since nums[i]>=0, greedy left-to-right packing is optimal to minimize count (cut only when forced). Search space is [max(nums), sum(nums)]. Binary search smallest feasible M gives minimal largest sum. This is parametric search.

timeComplexity.explanation: S = sum(nums). Each feasibility check is O(n) greedy scan, binary search needs O(log S) iterations (S up to 1e9, ~30 steps).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only counters and bounds besides input array.

steps: mid=21: greedy packs [7,2,5]=14, [10,8]=18 => 2 parts <=k feasible => hi=21
mid=15: packs [7,2,5]=14, [10]=10, [8]=8 => 3 parts >k not feasible => lo=16
check 18 feasible, 17 needs 3 parts, so answer 18

edgeCases: k==1: lo=max, hi=sum, check forces single part, returns sum
k==n: answer max(nums), greedy with M=max uses exactly n parts
single large element: lo ensures no M smaller than max element considered
all zeros: lo=0 hi=0 loop skipped, returns 0
